reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases; CDC parasitic disease guidance
clinicalPearls: A tissue-invasive infection caused by migrating larvae of the dog and cat roundworms Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati
Humans, especially young children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, are accidental hosts in which larvae cannot mature
The classic visceral form presents with fever, hepatomegaly, wheeze or cough, and marked eosinophilia
A separate ocular form causes unilateral visual loss, often mistaken for retinoblastoma, and typically lacks prominent eosinophilia
Diagnosis relies on serology (Toxocara-specific antibodies), as larvae are rarely recovered and stool examination is unhelpful because worms do not reach the gut in humans
A history of pica, geophagia, or close contact with puppies or contaminated environments supports the diagnosis
Most visceral disease is self-limiting; anthelmintics such as albendazole with corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction are used in significant or organ-threatening infection
Prevention centres on deworming pets, hand hygiene and reducing environmental soil contamination
reference.pathophysiology: Visceral larva migrans occurs when a human ingests embryonated Toxocara eggs from soil, faeces or contaminated food. The eggs hatch in the intestine and release larvae that penetrate the gut wall and migrate through the bloodstream to organs such as the liver, lungs, muscle, eye and brain. Because humans are not the natural host, the larvae cannot complete their life cycle or mature into adult worms; instead they persist and wander through tissues, provoking eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation and a strong immunoglobulin E response. The organ-specific symptoms and the intense eosinophilia reflect this larval migration and the host inflammatory reaction to it.
additionalDifferentials: Other tissue-migrating helminth infections (ascariasis, strongyloidiasis, hookworm)
Hepatic abscess or other focal liver lesions
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia
Liver ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging for hepatic and pulmonary lesions
Ophthalmological examination when ocular disease is suspected
Exclusion of other tissue-invasive helminths and haematological causes of eosinophilia
redFlags: Neurological features suggesting central nervous system involvement
Unilateral visual loss or leukocoria requiring urgent ophthalmological review
Persistent very high eosinophilia with systemic upset
reference.prognosis: The visceral form is usually self-limiting with a good outcome, but heavy or organ-threatening infection, and particularly ocular or central nervous system disease, can cause lasting damage such as permanent visual impairment.
pitfalls: Examining stool for ova, which is futile because the parasite does not mature in humans
Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with eosinophilia and pica or puppy contact
Relying on a single serology result without clinical correlation
Neglecting anti-inflammatory cover when treating heavy infection with anthelmintics
management: Anthelmintic therapy with albendazole, or mebendazole, to kill migrating Toxocara larvae in symptomatic visceral disease
Corticosteroids alongside anthelmintics for severe inflammation and for ocular or central nervous system involvement
Ophthalmological management of ocular toxocariasis with corticosteroids and, where needed, laser or vitreoretinal surgery
Symptomatic support such as bronchodilators for wheeze in the pulmonary form
Monitor eosinophilia and clinical response, with Toxocara serology to support the diagnosis
Prevention through regular deworming of pets, hand hygiene, and avoidance of pica and geophagia in young children
